Cataloging, database management, transcribing, storage and maintenance - sign me up! In a place where I can actually make a living. Of which there is little to none.

Librarian here. Some things to consider before you enroll in an LIS school: Competition for jobs is fierce, particularly in slow economies (budgets of libraries are very susceptible to be cut). You might want to focus your coursework in a very specific area (Cataloging, archives, management, etc.) so you will have more experience in the field you want. Also, take your time getting your MLIS. I made the mistake of completing two years' worth of classes in eighteen months, later realizing how many entry-level jobs are only open to current LIS students. (I'm essentially being penalized for having too strong a work ethic. But I digress.) And be sure to network.

More often than not, when a patron has lost or misplaced a book they will find it a few months later and return it. Having to deal with a book that has no record is not something automated and requires dedicated time and effort. Library's are almost always the most underfunded part of whatever community/organization they are apart of, so that kind of thing can have a significant negative impact on an ILL program. The Library I work at prides ourselves on a turn around time of a couple days or less, but most other and larger libraries can take 2 or more weeks to process and ship an item.

But like I said, that's only for ILL. For the same reasons most US libraries only keep a record of who last checked out a book. At our library there is no way for us to give a patron their check out history because we don't record or store that information once the transaction is complete.
